single-number.pattern: XOR cancellation: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x

approaches.name: Count each value with a nested loop
approaches.idea: For each element, count how many times it appears in the array; the one that appears once is the answer.
steps: For each index `i`, scan the whole array counting elements equal to `nums[i]`.
approaches.why: n scans of length n.

approaches.name: Hash map of counts
approaches.idea: Count every value in one pass, then return the one with count 1.
steps: Return the key whose count is 1.
approaches.why: Linear time, but the map breaks the O(1) extra-space requirement.

approaches.name: XOR everything
approaches.idea: XOR is commutative and associative, `x ^ x = 0` and `x ^ 0 = x`. XOR-ing the whole array cancels every pair and leaves the single value.
steps: XOR every element into it and return `result`.
approaches.why: One pass and one variable. Works for negative numbers too, since XOR acts bit by bit.

number-of-1-bits.pattern: Bit tricks: n & (n − 1) clears the lowest set bit

approaches.name: Write it out in binary and count the 1s
approaches.idea: Convert the 32-bit pattern to a binary string and count the `1` characters.
steps: Turn the value into its unsigned 32-bit binary string.
approaches.why: w = 32 characters are built and scanned. Negative inputs need the unsigned view: `& 0xFFFFFFFF` in Python, `>>> 0` in JavaScript.

approaches.name: Check all 32 bits
approaches.idea: Look at each bit position with a shift and a mask.
steps: For `i` from 0 to 31: add `(n >>> i) & 1` to the count.
approaches.why: Exactly 32 iterations, no extra memory. The unsigned shift `>>>` keeps the sign bit from smearing across.

approaches.name: Brian Kernighan: clear the lowest set bit
approaches.idea: `n & (n − 1)` removes exactly the lowest 1 bit, so the loop runs once per set bit instead of once per bit position.
approaches.why: k = number of set bits (≤ 32). C++ uses `unsigned` so `n − 1` cannot overflow at INT_MIN; Python masks to 32 bits first.

power-of-two.pattern: A power of two has exactly one set bit, so n & (n − 1) == 0

approaches.name: Keep dividing by 2
approaches.idea: A positive power of two reaches 1 when repeatedly halved, without ever hitting an odd number above 1.
approaches.why: At most 31 halvings.

approaches.name: Count the set bits
approaches.idea: A positive number is a power of two exactly when it has a single 1 bit.
approaches.why: Bit counting looks at up to w = 32 bits (often one hardware instruction).

approaches.name: n & (n − 1) == 0
approaches.idea: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and every bit below it. If that was the only set bit, `n & (n − 1)` is 0.
steps: The `n > 0` check rules out 0 and every negative number (including −2³¹, whose only set bit is the sign bit).
approaches.why: Two operations, no loop.

missing-number.pattern: XOR (or Gauss sum) of indices against values

approaches.name: Search for each candidate
approaches.idea: Try every value 0..n and scan the array to see whether it is there.
steps: For `v` from 0 to n: scan `nums` for `v`.
Return the first `v` that is not found.
approaches.why: n + 1 candidates, each a linear scan.

approaches.name: Hash set
approaches.idea: Put every value in a set, then check 0..n against it in O(1) each.
steps: Insert all of `nums` into a set.
Return the first `v` in 0..n not in the set.
approaches.why: Linear time but O(n) extra memory.

approaches.name: Cyclic sort: value v belongs at index v
approaches.idea: Values are 0..n in n slots, so every value except n has a home index equal to itself. Swap each value home and leave n wherever it lands; the slot that does not hold its own index is the missing number.
steps: While `i < n`: let `home = nums[i]`. If `home < n` and `nums[home] != nums[i]`, swap them (and stay at `i`); otherwise `i++`.
Return the first `i` with `nums[i] != i`, or `n` if every slot is right.
approaches.why: Each swap sends one value home for good, so there are at most n swaps. It changes the array, which XOR does not, but it is the version that still works when several numbers are missing (see the Cyclic Sort lesson).

approaches.name: XOR indices with values
approaches.idea: XOR together every index 0..n and every value. Each present number appears twice (once as an index, once as a value) and cancels; only the missing number is left.
steps: Start with `result = n` (the one index that has no array slot).
approaches.why: One pass, one variable. Equivalent alternative: `n(n + 1)/2 − sum(nums)`; XOR has no overflow risk in fixed-width languages.

approaches.name: Count bits of each number separately
approaches.idea: For each i from 0 to n, count its 1 bits with a loop.
steps: For each `i`, repeatedly add `x & 1` and shift `x` right until it is 0.
approaches.why: Each number takes O(log i) shifts. Space excludes the output array.

approaches.name: Reuse the answer for i >> 1
approaches.idea: `i >> 1` is `i` without its last bit, and it is smaller, so its count is already known. Add back the last bit.
approaches.why: O(1) per number. (`ans[i] = ans[i & (i − 1)] + 1` works the same way, by dropping the lowest set bit.)

reverse-bits.pattern: Bit shifting: pull bits off one end and push them onto the other (or swap halves with masks)

approaches.name: Reverse the 32-character binary string
approaches.idea: Write the value as exactly 32 binary digits, reverse the string, and parse it back as an unsigned 32-bit number, reinterpreted as a signed int.
steps: Build the 32-digit binary string (padding with leading zeros).
Reverse it and parse it base 2.
approaches.why: w = 32 characters are built, reversed and parsed.

approaches.name: Move the bits one at a time
approaches.idea: Take bits off the low end of `n` and push them onto the low end of the result, shifting the result left each time. After 32 steps the first bit taken is at the top.
approaches.why: Exactly w = 32 iterations, no strings.

approaches.name: Swap halves with masks (divide and conquer)
approaches.idea: Reversing 32 bits = swap the two 16-bit halves, then swap the bytes inside each half, then the nibbles, then bit pairs, then single bits. Each level is one mask-and-shift for all positions at once.
approaches.why: log₂ 32 = 5 rounds of a few operations, no loop. This is what `Integer.reverse` does internally.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def reverseBits(self, n: int) -> int:
        n &= 0xFFFFFFFF
        n = ((n >> 16) | (n << 16)) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        n = ((n & 0xff00ff00) >> 8) | ((n & 0x00ff00ff) << 8)
        n = ((n & 0xf0f0f0f0) >> 4) | ((n & 0x0f0f0f0f) << 4)
        n = ((n & 0xcccccccc) >> 2) | ((n & 0x33333333) << 2)
        n = ((n & 0xaaaaaaaa) >> 1) | ((n & 0x55555555) << 1)
        return n - (1 << 32) if n >= 1 << 31 else n

single-number-ii.pattern: Per-bit counting modulo 3, compressed into a two-variable state machine (ones, twos)

approaches.name: Count each value with a nested loop
approaches.idea: For each element, count its occurrences; return the one that appears once.
steps: For each value, scan the array counting equal elements.
Return it when the count is 1.
approaches.why: n scans of length n.

approaches.name: Hash map of counts
approaches.idea: Count every value in one pass and return the one with count 1.
steps: Return the key whose count is 1.
approaches.why: Linear time, but O(n) extra memory.

approaches.name: Count each bit modulo 3
approaches.idea: For every bit position, the values appearing three times contribute a multiple of 3 set bits. So `count % 3` at each position is exactly the single value's bit.
steps: For each of the 32 bit positions, count how many numbers have that bit set.
If `count % 3 == 1`, set that bit in the result.
The sign bit is handled like any other in 32-bit arithmetic (Python converts the 32-bit pattern back to a signed value).
approaches.why: 32 passes over the array, constant memory.

approaches.name: ones / twos state machine
approaches.idea: Track, for all 32 bits at once, whether each bit has been seen 1 time (`ones`) or 2 times (`twos`) modulo 3. A third occurrence clears both. What survives in `ones` is the single value.
approaches.why: One pass, two variables — the bit-count idea with each per-bit counter (0 → 1 → 2 → 0) stored across the two words.

sum-of-two-integers.pattern: Binary addition: XOR is the sum without carries, AND shifted left is the carry

approaches.name: Ripple-carry adder, one bit at a time
approaches.idea: Do what a hardware adder does: for each of the 32 positions, the sum bit is `a ^ b ^ carry`, and the carry into the next position is set when at least two of the three are set.
steps: Walk a one-bit mask from bit 0 to bit 31 (stop when shifting it pushes it out).
At each position: `x = a & bit`, `y = b & bit`; result gets `x ^ y ^ carry`.
Next carry = `(x & y | x & carry | y & carry) << 1`.
approaches.why: Always w = 32 steps. Written without any `+` or `−` at all, including the loop.

approaches.name: XOR + carry loop on whole words
approaches.idea: Add all bits at once: `a ^ b` is the sum ignoring carries, `(a & b) << 1` is every carry. Add those two the same way until no carry is left.
steps: Python has unbounded integers, so mask to 32 bits each round and convert the final pattern back to a signed value.
approaches.why: Each round moves the lowest carry at least one position left, so at most 32 rounds — usually far fewer. C++ shifts as `unsigned` to avoid undefined behaviour on negative values.

single-number-iii.pattern: XOR, then split the array by one bit where the two singles differ

approaches.name: Count each value with a nested loop
approaches.idea: Count every element's occurrences and collect the two that appear once.
steps: For each value, scan the array counting equal elements.
approaches.why: n scans of length n (space excludes the two-element answer).

approaches.name: Hash map of counts
approaches.idea: Count values in one pass and return those with count 1.
approaches.why: Linear time, O(n) extra memory.

approaches.name: XOR and split on the lowest differing bit
approaches.idea: XOR of everything is `a ^ b` (pairs cancel). It is non-zero, so pick any set bit — the lowest, `x & −x`. `a` and `b` differ there, so splitting the array by that bit puts them in different groups, and each group's pairs still cancel.
steps: XOR the numbers with that bit set into `a`; the others into `b`.
approaches.why: Two passes, three variables. When `x` is −2³¹, `−x` overflows back to −2³¹ in Java/JS and `low` is still the right bit; C++ uses `unsigned` so the negation is well defined.

approaches.name: Convert to integers and back
approaches.idea: Parse both strings as binary numbers, add them, and print the sum in binary.
steps: Add them and convert the sum back to a binary string.
approaches.why: Inputs can have 10⁴ bits, while a 64-bit integer holds 63. The long tests overflow in Java, C++ and JavaScript (Python's big integers survive, but that dodges the point of the exercise).

approaches.name: Two pointers from the right with a carry
approaches.idea: Add the strings like grade-school addition: walk both from the last bit, add the bits and the carry, write the low bit, and carry the high bit.
steps: Set `i`, `j` to the last indices and `carry = 0`.
While `i >= 0`, `j >= 0` or `carry > 0`: `sum = carry + bit(a, i) + bit(b, j)`; append `sum % 2`; `carry = sum / 2`; move both pointers left.
Reverse the appended bits and return them.
approaches.why: One pass over the longer string; the output needs at most one extra bit. Looping while the carry is non-zero handles "1" + "1" = "10" without a special case.

bitwise-and-of-numbers-range.pattern: Common binary prefix of left and right

approaches.name: AND every number
approaches.idea: Start with `left` and AND in every number up to `right`, stopping early once the result reaches 0.
steps: For `k` from `left + 1` to `right` (as a 64-bit counter), set `r &= k`; break if `r == 0`.
approaches.why: The early exit helps when the range crosses a power of two, but a range like [2³⁰, 2³¹ − 1] keeps a set bit the whole way through, about 10⁹ steps, so it times out there.

approaches.name: Clear the lowest set bit of right
approaches.idea: While `right > left`, remove right's lowest set bit (`right & (right − 1)`). Each removal drops a bit that must vary inside the range.
approaches.why: At most 31 iterations. If right is still larger than left, the number right − 1 is in the range and differs from right in its lowest set bit, so that bit cannot survive the AND.

approaches.name: Shift to the common prefix
approaches.idea: Bits below the highest position where `left` and `right` differ all take both values somewhere in the range, so they AND to 0. Only the shared prefix survives.
steps: Shift `left` and `right` right together, counting shifts, until they are equal.
Shift the common value back left by that count.
approaches.why: At most 31 shifts. Between two numbers that differ at bit k there is a number ending in 0111…1 and the next one ending in 1000…0, which together zero out every bit up to k.

minimum-array-end.pattern: Write n − 1 into the zero bits of x

approaches.name: Step to the next valid number n − 1 times
approaches.idea: Start at `x`. The next valid element is the smallest larger number that still contains all of x's bits: `(cur + 1) | x`. Apply that `n − 1` times.
approaches.why: Adding 1 and OR-ing x back in jumps straight over every number missing one of x's bits, so each step is O(1). Still, n can be 10⁸, which is too slow for the largest tests.

approaches.name: Deposit the bits of n − 1
approaches.idea: Valid numbers are x with any pattern in its 0-bit positions, and they are ordered by that pattern. The (n − 1)-th one (counting from 0) puts the binary digits of n − 1 into those free positions, lowest first.
steps: Walk bit positions upward. Skip positions where x has a 1. At each free position, copy the lowest bit of `rest` into `result`, then shift `rest` right.
approaches.why: At most about 60 bit positions are visited. The answer can exceed 2³¹ (for example n = x = 10⁸), so it must be computed in 64 bits; in JavaScript, plain numbers are safe up to 2⁵³ but bitwise operators work on 32 bits, so the code uses arithmetic or BigInt.
